examples: 어제 올라온 공지를 확인했어요.
I checked the notice posted yesterday.
The modifier 올라온 identifies which notice.
nuance: 공지 is more official than a casual message. It often hides the actor and foregrounds the posted information.
mistakes: Do not translate every notice sentence as a full who-did-it sentence; first find the final noun.

examples: 변경된 일정이 공지에 나왔어요.
The changed schedule appeared in the notice.
The sentence focuses on the changed schedule, not who changed it.
nuance: 변경된 focuses on the resulting state. It sounds natural in notices, emails, and announcements.
mistakes: Do not separate it into 변경됐어요 일정; Korean puts the modifier before the noun.

english: to be read / to make someone read
examples: 저는 그 문장이 처음에 잘 안 읽혔어요.
At first, that sentence did not read clearly to me.
The text is the focus.
nuance: With texts, 읽히다 often describes how easily something is read or understood.
mistakes: Do not pair 읽히다 with a plain active example like 책을 읽어요 when teaching this chapter.

examples: 인기 상품이 하루 만에 다 팔렸어요.
The popular product sold out in one day.
The product is the subject.
nuance: Use 팔리다 when the seller is not important or not known.
mistakes: Do not use 팔다 when the product itself should be the subject.

english: to be set / to be scheduled
examples: 회의 일정이 다음 주로 잡혔어요.
The meeting schedule was set for next week.
The sentence focuses on the schedule result.
nuance: 잡히다 is natural for appointments, schedules, reservations, and plans.
mistakes: Do not translate it literally as “be grabbed” in schedule contexts.

examples: 문이 자동으로 닫혔어요.
The door closed automatically.
The door is the subject.
nuance: Use 닫히다 when you care about the closed state/result more than the person closing it.
mistakes: 닫다 needs an actor; 닫히다 lets the object become the subject.

english: to feed / to make someone take
examples: 엄마가 아이에게 약을 먹였어요.
The mother gave the child medicine.
Someone causes another person to take something.
nuance: The subject is the causer, not the person eating.
mistakes: Do not use 먹다 when the subject is making another person eat.

usage: to seat someone in the front row
examples: 직원이 손님을 창가 자리에 앉혔어요.
The staff seated the guest by the window.
The staff causes the guest to sit.
nuance: 앉다 is what the person does; 앉히다 is what someone else does to seat them.
mistakes: Do not say 손님을 앉았어요; use 손님을 앉혔어요.

english: to dress someone / put clothing on someone
usage: to put a coat on a child
examples: 아버지가 아기에게 코트를 입혔어요.
The father put a coat on the baby.
Someone causes another person to wear clothing.
nuance: 입다 is wear; 입히다 is dress someone else.
mistakes: Do not use 입다 when the subject is dressing another person.

examples: 한글은 소리 글자예요.
Hangul is a sound-based writing system.
This is the core sentence of Chapter 1.
nuance: Say 한글 for the writing system, 한국어 for the language. This chapter is about the writing system first.
mistakes: Do not treat romanization as Korean spelling. Read the Hangul first, then use romanization only to check.

examples: ㄱ은 자음이에요.
ㄱ is a consonant.
Use this frame to label letters.
nuance: A consonant can sit at the beginning of a block, and some consonants can also sit at the bottom as 받침.
mistakes: Do not read the consonant names as if they were English letter names. Listen and imitate the Korean names.

examples: ㅏ는 모음이에요.
ㅏ is a vowel.
ㅏ is a tall vowel that sits to the right.
nuance: The visual direction of a vowel helps the learner remember the mouth shape.
mistakes: Do not put a tall vowel below the consonant; tall vowels sit to the right.

examples: 이 글자가 뭐예요?
What is this character?
A survival question for the first lesson.
nuance: 글자 can mean an individual written unit. In this chapter it usually points to a Hangul block or letter being studied.
mistakes: Do not assume every visible shape equals one English-style letter; a Hangul block can contain two or three letters.

examples: 이 글자의 소리가 뭐예요?
What is the sound of this character?
Ask this when the shape is new.
nuance: 소리 points to what you hear, while 글자 points to what you see.
mistakes: Do not read romanization with English habits and call that the sound. Listen to the Korean sound.

examples: 이건 제 명함이에요.
This is my business card.
A natural first-meeting object sentence.
nuance: Use 이건 when the thing is near you or already visible in the conversation.
mistakes: Do not say 이는 뭐예요. Use 이건 뭐예요 in everyday speech.

examples: 제 이름은 민수예요.
My name is Minsu.
이름 ends in a consonant, so it takes 은 as the topic marker.
nuance: 제 sounds polite and safe. 내 is casual and belongs with close friends or informal speech.
mistakes: Do not use 내 in a first meeting unless the relationship is already casual.

english: is not / am not / are not
usage: 학생 ends in a consonant, so use 이 before 아니에요.
의사 ends in a vowel, so use 가 before 아니에요.
사람 ends in a consonant, so use 이.
examples: 저는 선생님이 아니에요. 학생이에요.
I am not a teacher. I am a student.
This contrasts one identity with another.
nuance: 아니에요 negates noun labels. It is not the same as 없어요, which means something does not exist or you do not have it.
mistakes: Do not stack 이에요 and 아니에요 together. Say 학생이 아니에요, not 학생이에요 아니에요.

examples: 이건 한국어예요.
This is Korean.
Use this when identifying a sentence, label, or language.
nuance: 한국어 points to the language. 한국 사람 points to a Korean person.
mistakes: Do not use 한국어 when you mean a Korean person. Say 한국 사람.

examples: 제 직업은 영어 선생님이에요.
My job is English teacher.
선생님 ends in a consonant, so the sentence ends with 이에요.
nuance: 영어 is the language. 미국 사람 means an American person.
mistakes: Do not use 영어 사람 for an English-speaking person. Use 미국 사람, 영국 사람, or another nationality as needed.

usage: 시간 ends in a consonant, so use 이.
자리 ends in a vowel, so use 가.
A common restaurant and hotel question.
examples: 여기 화장실이 있어요?
Is there a bathroom here?
The question word order stays the same; intonation makes it a question.
nuance: 있어요 can mean both 'there is' and 'have.' Context tells whether the sentence is about existence or possession.
mistakes: Do not use 을/를 with 있어요. Say 시간이 있어요, not 시간을 있어요.

english: there is not / do not have
usage: same subject particle as 시간이 있어요
문제 ends in a vowel, so use 가.
I do not have a reservation.
Useful for walk-in restaurant or hotel situations.
examples: 지금 돈이 없어요.
I do not have money right now.
돈 ends in a consonant, so use 이.
nuance: 없어요 negates existence or possession. It is not the same as 아니에요, which negates a noun identity.
mistakes: Do not say 예약을 없어요. The reservation is the subject of absence: 예약이 없어요.

usage: 예약 ends in ㄱ, so use 이.
I do not have a reservation.
same noun and particle, opposite verb
staff often use the honorific 있으세요 with customers.
examples: 예약이 없어요. 자리가 있어요?
I do not have a reservation. Is there a seat?
A natural walk-in restaurant line.
nuance: 예약 is the noun. 예약하다 is the verb 'to reserve/book.' In this chapter, focus first on the noun with 있어요/없어요.
mistakes: Do not use 예약을 with 있어요/없어요. Use 예약이 because the reservation is the thing that exists.

usage: I want to go to the Han River.
Can you go to the Han River?
가다 becomes 갈 수 있어요 in the ability/possibility pattern.
examples: 이번 주말에 한강에 갈 수 있어요.
I can go to the Han River this weekend.
A natural weekend plan sentence for Chapter 8.
nuance: Use 한강 as a destination with 에, not 에서, when the main verb is 가다.
mistakes: Do not say 한강에서 가요 for destination. Use 한강에 가요.

usage: Ask this when you need a staff desk in a station or museum.
Please ask at the information desk.
에서 marks the place where the asking happens.
examples: 안내소는 오전 9시부터 오후 6시까지 열어요.
The information desk is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
A clean Chapter 10 time-range sentence with 부터/까지.
nuance: 안내소 is a place, so use 에 for location and 에서 for asking or receiving help there.
mistakes: Do not use 안내소부터 when you simply mean 'at the information desk.' Use 안내소에서.

usage: Where is the place to take Line 2?
타는 곳 = boarding place / platform area.
Which exit side is Line 2 toward?
Useful in large subway stations with many exits.
examples: 2호선 타는 곳은 5번 출구 쪽이에요.
The Line 2 boarding area is toward exit 5.
A natural station-help answer.
nuance: Koreans often give subway directions by line number plus exit number or direction.
mistakes: Do not say 2호선은 5번 출구예요 if you mean the boarding area. Say 2호선 타는 곳은 5번 출구 쪽이에요.

usage: I think the pacing is slow.
느리다 is an adjective, so use 느린 것 같아요.
examples: 전개가 너무 느리잖아요.
The pacing is too slow, you know.
-잖아요 reminds the listener of something both viewers just experienced.
nuance: Use 전개 for the flow of a story or argument, not for a person's speed.
mistakes: Do not translate pacing literally as 속도 in movie-review sentences when you mean story development. 전개 is more natural.

usage: I think the ending is a bit disappointing.
아쉽다 becomes 아쉬운 before 것 같아요.
examples: 결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요.
I thought the ending felt a bit rushed.
Past impression: 것 같았어요.
nuance: 결말 is about narrative ending; 끝 is more general and less review-like.
mistakes: Do not overuse 끝 for movie-review nuance. 결말 sounds more natural for story endings.

usage: I think the acting seems natural.
examples: 배우들 연기는 정말 좋았잖아요.
The actors' performances were really good, you know.
-잖아요 works because both people saw the same acting.
nuance: 연기 is the noun; 연기하다 is the verb 'to act/perform.'
mistakes: Do not confuse 연기 'acting' with 연기 'smoke' in other contexts; movie/drama context makes the meaning clear.

usage: The lead actor is really good, you see.
-거든요 gives this as supporting background for the speaker's opinion.
examples: 주인공이 너무 완벽한 것 같아요.
I think the main character is too perfect.
완벽하다 becomes 완벽한 before 것 같아요.
nuance: 주인공 can refer to a fictional main character or the lead person in a real event.
mistakes: Do not use 배우 when you mean the character inside the story; use 주인공 for protagonist, 배우 for actor.

usage: Personally, I like open endings, you see.
A natural way to explain a different preference without sounding confrontational.
examples: 개인적으로는 좀 아쉬운 것 같아요.
Personally, I think it's a bit disappointing.
Double softening: personally + seems.
nuance: 개인적으로 does not mean privately here; it marks a personal opinion.
mistakes: Do not combine 개인적으로는 저는 unless you need strong contrast. Usually 개인적으로는 alone is enough.

usage: Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
-거든요 gives the honest feeling as background.
examples: 솔직히 말하면 결말이 급한 것 같았어요.
Honestly, I thought the ending felt rushed.
솔직히 말하면 + 것 같았어요 softens a direct critique.
nuance: 솔직히 is more direct than 개인적으로, so pair it with softer grammar when criticizing.
mistakes: Do not use 솔직히 as a license to be blunt; Korean still often needs softening after it.

english: to be / to stay (honorific for a person's presence)
usage: The professor is in the office.
A respected person's physical presence uses 계시다.
examples: 팀장님이 지금 자리에 안 계세요.
The team lead is not at their desk right now.
안 계세요 is the natural negative for a respected person's location.
nuance: 있으세요 can be used for possessions or states, but 계세요 is the respectful choice for where a person is.
mistakes: For a teacher or elder's location, say 어디에 계세요? instead of 어디에 있으세요?

usage: I gave my parents a gift.
께 plus 드리다 marks the respectful direction of the giving.
examples: 제가 팀장님께 자료를 드릴게요.
I'll give the materials to the team lead.
A useful office sentence that pairs naturally with reported speech.
nuance: 드리다 is about humble direction: I give upward. If the senior person gives to you, use 주시다 instead.
mistakes: Do not use 드리다 just because the sentence is polite; use it when the recipient is someone you honor.

english: to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)
usage: I explained the situation to the professor.
This is more natural than 교수님께 말했어요 in a respectful context.
examples: 팀장님께 참여하고 싶다고 말씀드릴게요.
I'll tell the team lead that I want to participate.
The reported content uses -다고; the speaking verb is humble.
nuance: 말씀드리다 points upward to the listener. 말씀하시다 is used when the respected person speaks.
mistakes: Do not say 제가 말씀하셨어요. Use 제가 말씀드렸어요 for your humble action.

english: to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)
usage: Could I meet the professor tomorrow?
뵐 is the future/modifying form of 뵙다.
examples: 처음 뵙겠습니다.
It's nice to meet you for the first time.
A fixed formal first-meeting greeting.
nuance: 뵙다 is humble: it lowers your action of meeting so the other person is respected.
mistakes: For friends, use 만나다 or 보다; 뵙다 is too formal for equal casual relationships.

usage: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
진지 is also honorific vocabulary for 밥.
examples: 할아버지께서 아침을 잡수셨어요.
Grandfather ate breakfast.
께서 plus 잡수셨어요 marks high respect.
nuance: 드시다 is the safer everyday honorific for eating; 잡수시다 sounds very respectful and elder-focused.
mistakes: Do not use 잡수시다 for yourself.

usage: 하마터면 adds the near-miss alarm feeling.
examples: 하마터면 지갑을 잃어버릴 뻔했어요.
I almost lost my wallet.
A common everyday close-call sentence.
nuance: 하마터면 is dramatic but natural when the speaker feels relieved that the event did not happen.
mistakes: Do not use 하마터면 alone; pair it with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요.

english: to tremble / to feel nervous and shaky
usage: My voice shook during the presentation.
examples: 너무 긴장해서 울 뻔했어요.
I was so nervous I almost cried.
떨리다 often appears near close-call emotion sentences like 울 뻔했어요.
nuance: 떨리다 can be physical shaking or the nervous feeling behind it.
mistakes: Do not use 떨다 for every nervous feeling; 떨리다 is the more natural intransitive form for 'my voice/hands/heart shake.'

usage: The more you practice, the more your skill improves.
examples: 한국어를 쓸수록 실력이 늘어요.
The more you use Korean, the more your ability improves.
실력이 늘다 is the natural collocation.
nuance: 실력 is not confidence or effort; it is the ability itself.
mistakes: Say 실력이 늘어요 for ability improving, not 실력이 커요.

english: because of / as a result of an unexpected problem
usage: The appointment got canceled because it rained.
The rain is the disruptive cause.
examples: 갑자기 일이 생기는 바람에 못 갔어요.
I could not go because something suddenly came up.
A very common excuse/explanation frame.
nuance: 바람에 usually carries a negative or inconvenient result, unlike neutral -아서/어서.
mistakes: Do not use 바람에 for happy planned reasons. For purpose, use -기 위해서.

usage: A natural way to say something suits your personal preference.
Useful when comparing preferences without arguing.
취향에 맞다 is a very common collocation.
examples: 저는 조용한 카페가 제 취향이에요.
Quiet cafes are my taste.
Connects preference with a descriptive noun phrase.
우리는 영화 취향이 조금 달라요.
Our movie tastes are a little different.
Common with 영화, 음악, 음식, 옷, and 카페.
nuance: 취향 is subjective. 좋아해요 states a preference, while 취향 names the style or taste behind that preference.
mistakes: Do not use 취향 for every objective choice. For price, distance, or time, use comparison expressions instead.
취향 is usually paired with 이/가 or 에: 취향이 달라요, 취향에 맞아요.

examples: 다른 색도 추천해 주세요.
Please recommend another color too.
Useful in shopping after trying something on.
nuance: 추천하다 is neutral and practical. In speech, 추천해 주세요 is much more useful than the dictionary form.
mistakes: Do not use 추천하다 alone as a request. Say 추천해 주세요.
The recommended item usually takes 을/를: 식당을 추천하다, 색을 추천하다.

usage: A soft encouragement, not a hard command.
Should I try it on once?
examples: 이 옷 한번 입어 보세요.
Try on these clothes once.
한번 makes the suggestion feel low-pressure.
nuance: 한번 does not always literally mean one time. With -아/어 보다, it often means 'just give it a try.'
mistakes: Do not over-translate 한번 as exactly one time in every sentence.
For spacing, both 한 번 and 한번 appear, but this course treats the conversational chunk 한번 해 보세요 as one useful expression.

english: to be okay; to be fine
usage: It is okay / I am okay.
Common response to offers, suggestions, and concern.
examples: 사이즈가 괜찮으면 이걸로 할게요.
If the size is okay, I will take this one.
Common shop decision frame.
nuance: 괜찮아요 can mean okay, fine, no thanks, or not bad. Context decides.
mistakes: Do not assume 괜찮아요 always means yes. After an offer, 아니요, 괜찮아요 can mean no thanks.
For a direct recommendation, use 좋아요 or 추천해요; 괜찮아요 can sound milder, like 'it's okay.'

english: to not matter; to be okay either way
usage: Common answer when either choice is okay.
It is okay even if it is expensive.
-아/어도 plus 상관없다 is a useful concession frame.
examples: 조금 늦어도 상관없어요.
It does not matter even if we are a little late.
The outcome stays okay despite the condition.
nuance: 상관없다 is neutral and practical. It can sound indifferent, so use 괜찮아요 when you want a warmer tone.
mistakes: Do not use 상관없다 when you actually have a strong preference.
The condition often appears with -아/어도: 늦어도 상관없어요.

usage: I think I will be a little late.
Soft warning before you arrive late.
I guess the reply is late.
examples: 길이 막혀서 좀 늦을지도 몰라요.
Traffic is heavy, so I might be a bit late.
-ㄹ지도 몰라요 leaves the possibility open.
nuance: 늦다 is a descriptive verb, so it behaves like an adjective in Korean. Use 늦게 for the adverb 'late': 늦게 왔어요.
mistakes: Do not use 늦게 when the sentence needs 'be late': 늦을 것 같아요, not 늦게 것 같아요.
For a delayed reply, 답장이 늦다 is natural.

usage: There is a chance it will rain.
A more noun-based way to talk about probability.
Useful when you are not fully ruling something out.
examples: 늦을 가능성이 있으니까 먼저 주문해요.
There is a chance they will be late, so let's order first.
가능성 gives the reason for a practical decision.
nuance: 가능성 is a noun, so it pairs with 있다, 없다, 높다, and 낮다. It is a little more formal than just saying -ㄹ지도 몰라요.
mistakes: Do not use 가능하다 when you mean 'chance' as a noun. Say 가능성이 있어요.
가능성이 높아요 means 'it is likely,' not 'the ability is high.'

usage: A simple way to say the guess is not random.
We can guess from this clue.
The clue takes 로 when it is the basis or means.
examples: 하늘이 흐린 게 첫 번째 단서예요.
The cloudy sky is the first clue.
A concrete clue before a weather inference.
nuance: 단서 is more everyday and lighter than 증거 when you are only guessing. 증거 sounds more like evidence or proof.
mistakes: Do not say 단서하다. Use 단서가 있다 or 단서로 추측하다.
Use 증거 when you mean proof; use 단서 when you only have a clue.

usage: 로 marks the basis or means.
A useful hedge when you are not sure.
examples: 우산을 보고 비가 오나 봐요라고 추측했어요.
I saw the umbrella and guessed, 'It looks like it is raining.'
The visible object supports the inference.
nuance: 추측하다 is more explicit than -나 봐요. In conversation, the pattern often does the work, and 추측하다 names the thinking process.
mistakes: Do not use 추측하다 for facts you already know.
In casual speech, 너무 추측했어요 can sound odd; say 그냥 추측이에요.

examples: 비가 금방 그칠 것 같아요.
I think the rain will stop soon.
-ㄹ 것 같아요 makes a soft prediction.
nuance: 그치다 is intransitive: 비가 그쳐요. If you stop doing an action yourself, use 멈추다 or 그만하다 depending on the sentence.
mistakes: Do not say 비를 그쳐요 for 'the rain stops.' The rain takes 이/가: 비가 그쳐요.
그치다 is especially common with rain and snow.

usage: Noun plus 중 compresses the current activity.
Verb plus -는 중 emphasizes being mid-action.
examples: 전화 중이라 잠깐만 기다려 주세요.
I am on a call, so please wait a moment.
중이라 gives the reason from the current activity.
nuance: 중 feels more immediate than broad -고 있어요. It often sounds like 'right in the middle of it.'
mistakes: Do not attach 중 directly to adjectives: 바쁜 중이에요 is unnatural for 'I am busy.' Say 바빠요 or 일하는 중이에요.
With verbs, use the modifier: 먹는 중이에요, not 먹다 중이에요.

usage: I read a book while waiting.
Two actions overlap during the same span.
I could not see the message during the meeting.
The meeting is the time span.
examples: 한 시간 동안 한국어를 공부했어요.
I studied Korean for one hour.
A duration noun can come before 동안.
nuance: 동안 is about overlapping time or duration. It does not mean the contrastive English 'while' in sentences like 'while this is cheap, that is expensive.'
mistakes: Use V-는 동안, not V-은 동안: 자는 동안, 공부하는 동안.
For a point in time, use 때; for the whole span, use 동안.

usage: Useful when asking about the next step.
First I wash, and then I eat breakfast.
먼저 and 그다음 make the sequence easy to follow.
examples: 예약을 확인하고 나서 그다음 방으로 올라갔어요.
After checking the reservation, I went up to the room next.
그다음 names the following step after a completed action.
nuance: 그다음 is conversational and clear. In writing, 그 후 or 이후 can sound more formal.
mistakes: Do not use 그다음 as a noun for 'the next person' unless the context is clear.
For immediate timing, use -자마자 or 바로, not only 그다음.

usage: A direct match for a changed plan.
I got a call midway while going.
examples: 공부하다가 중간에 잠깐 쉬었어요.
I took a short break in the middle of studying.
The original action pauses before it is finished.
nuance: 중간에 does not always mean the exact mathematical center. It often means midway or before the process was finished.
mistakes: Do not use 중간에 for a completed first action. If the first action finished, use -고 나서.
For a location physically between two places, 중간 is a noun; this card focuses on timing.

usage: The window became open and remains that way.
examples: 카페 문이 아직 열려 있어요.
The cafe door is still open.
아직 plus result-state is very natural.
nuance: 열다 needs an actor opening something. 열리다 lets the opened thing become the subject.
mistakes: Do not say 문을 열려 있어요. The thing in the state takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Use 열고 있어요 only when someone is actively opening it right now.

english: to turn on; to be turned on
examples: 방에 불이 켜져 있어서 누가 있는 줄 알았어요.
The light was on in the room, so I thought someone was there.
Result-state gives the visual clue.
nuance: 켜다 is the action of turning something on. 켜지다 focuses on the thing becoming or being on.
mistakes: Do not say 불을 켜져 있어요. Say 불이 켜져 있어요.
Use 켜고 있어요 only when someone is in the act of turning it on.

usage: for employment / in order to get a job
Common compound for preparing to get hired.
to succeed in getting a job
examples: 취업을 위해서 매일 한국어를 연습해요.
I practice Korean every day in order to get a job.
Purpose plus daily practice.
방학 동안 취업 준비를 할 거예요.
I will prepare for job hunting during vacation.
Duration plus practical goal.
nuance: 취업 is the process or result of getting employment. 직업 is your occupation or job type, and 회사 is the company. For a purpose sentence, 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서 is natural.
mistakes: Do not use 직업을 위해서 when you mean 'to get a job'. Use 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서.
Do not drop the object particle in the learner frame. Say 취업을 위해서, not 취업 위해서, until the full pattern feels natural.

usage: Natural polite everyday style after the formal presentation is done.
May I ask the teacher a question?
examples: 친구가 아니면 처음에는 해요체로 말하는 게 안전해요.
If they are not a friend, it is safe to speak in haeyo style at first.
Practical social rule for learners.
nuance: 해요체 is polite conversation, not formal ceremony language. It sounds warmer and more natural than 합쇼체 in daily life.
mistakes: Using 합쇼체 with classmates after class can sound stiff or distant.
Using 반말 with someone you just met can sound rude even if the grammar is simple.

usage: I will begin the presentation now.
examples: 면접에서는 합쇼체로 말하는 게 자연스러워요.
In an interview, speaking in formal polite style sounds natural.
A real setting where 합쇼체 fits.
nuance: 합쇼체 overlaps with the name 하십시오체. Learners mainly need to recognize the endings -ㅂ니다/습니다, -ㅂ니까/습니까, and -(으)십시오.
mistakes: Using 합쇼체 everywhere because it feels 'more polite'. In everyday talk, it can sound too stiff.
Forgetting that ㄹ drops before ㅂ니다: 살다 becomes 삽니다.

usage: Can we speak casually to each other?
A common way to ask permission before switching.
I use casual speech with close friends.
examples: 처음 만난 사람에게 반말을 쓰면 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.
If you use casual speech with someone you just met, it can sound rude.
Social boundary.
nuance: 반말 is not 'bad Korean'. It is the right style in close relationships, but the wrong style in many public or first-meeting settings.
mistakes: Using 반말 with a teacher or staff member because the learner knows the short form.
Thinking 반말 equals friendly in every situation. Relationship and permission matter.

usage: I use polite speech with the teacher.
examples: 존댓말을 써도 상황에 따라 해요체와 합쇼체가 달라져요.
Even when using polite speech, haeyo style and formal style differ by situation.
Shows that 존댓말 is an umbrella term.
nuance: 존댓말 is about social respect. It does not automatically mean the most formal ending possible.
mistakes: Equating 존댓말 only with 합니다. 해요체 is also 존댓말.
Using honorific -(으)시- for yourself. Respectful speech and subject honorifics are related but not identical.

usage: What way of speaking should I use?
examples: 발표에서는 말투를 조금 더 격식 있게 바꿔야 해요.
In a presentation, you need to make your tone a little more formal.
Speech-level choice as a tone adjustment.
nuance: 말투 can describe grammar level, but also attitude. A sentence can be grammatically polite and still sound cold or awkward.
mistakes: Thinking only the verb ending matters. Particles, word choice, and directness also affect 말투.

usage: A key phrase for choosing 합쇼체.
examples: 면접은 격식 있는 자리라서 합쇼체가 자연스러워요.
An interview is a formal setting, so formal polite style sounds natural.
Connects setting to speech level.
nuance: 격식 is not just politeness. It is the formal frame expected by the setting.
mistakes: Using 격식 있는 말투 with close friends can sound distant or theatrical.

examples: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
The honored person is the topic of the sentence.
nuance: 높임말 is not only being polite to the listener. It can honor a third person, such as a teacher or parent.
mistakes: Using -(으)시- for yourself. Do not say 제가 가세요.
Thinking 존댓말 and 높임말 are always the same. They overlap, but they answer different social questions.

usage: Particle and verb both carry respect.
examples: 사장님께서 회의실에 계세요.
The boss is in the meeting room.
Respected subject plus 계시다.
nuance: 께서 honors the subject. It is not the same as 께, which means 'to' a respected person.
mistakes: Using 께서 for yourself: 제가께서 is impossible.
Confusing 께서 with 께. 선생님께서 오세요 but 선생님께 말씀드려요.

usage: I ask the teacher a question.
examples: 고객님께 먼저 안내해 드리겠습니다.
I will first guide the customer.
Formal service language.
nuance: 께 marks a respected recipient. 께서 marks a respected subject.
mistakes: Saying 선생님께서 질문해요 when you mean 'I ask the teacher'. Use 선생님께 질문해요.
Using 한테 in formal respectful contexts where 께 is expected.

usage: The teacher is in the classroom.
The boss is not here right now.
examples: 부모님은 집에 계세요.
My parents are at home.
Respectful way to talk about parents.
nuance: 계시다 replaces 있다 only for respected people. For things, use 있다: 가방이 있어요, not 가방이 계세요.
mistakes: Using 계시다 for objects or animals without a special respectful reason.
Using 있다 for a respected person in a context where honorifics are expected.

examples: 할머니께서 진지를 드세요.
Grandmother is eating.
Traditional respectful meal word plus honorific verb.
nuance: 드시다 honors the eater/drinker. It does not honor the food.
mistakes: Using 드시다 for your own eating: 제가 드세요 is wrong.
Thinking 드시다 means only 'eat'. It can also be used for drinking.

examples: 부모님은 보통 일찍 주무세요.
My parents usually sleep early.
Respectful family sentence.
nuance: 주무시다 is a special honorific verb. Do not build it mechanically from 자다.
mistakes: Saying 자세요 can be understandable, but 주무세요 is the standard respectful form.
Using 주무시다 for yourself.

examples: 어머니께서 먼저 말씀하셨어요.
My mother spoke first.
Honors mother as subject.
nuance: 말씀하시다 honors the speaker. 말씀드리다 humbles your act of telling someone respected.
mistakes: Confusing 말씀하시다 and 말씀드리다. The direction of respect is different.
Using 말하다 where 말씀하시다 is expected for a respected subject.

english: to give/do for a respected person (humble)
examples: 고객님께 다시 안내해 드리겠습니다.
I will guide the customer again.
Service-register humble helper.
nuance: 드리다 respects the recipient, not the subject. It is different from -(으)시-, which honors the subject.
mistakes: Saying 제가 오시다 or 제가 드세요 to be polite about yourself. Use 드리다 only when your action goes to someone respected.
Forgetting 께 before the respected recipient.

english: but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)
usage: But / by the way, are you free today?
But that is a little difficult, though.
examples: 근데 자료는 언제 보낼 수 있어요?
But when can you send the materials?
Spoken contrast in a team conversation.
nuance: 근데 is common in speech, but it can sound too casual in a presentation, email, or formal announcement.
mistakes: Using 근데 in formal writing where 그런데 is safer.
Using 근데 every sentence; it becomes filler if there is no real contrast or topic shift.

usage: Actually, I have not finished it yet.
사실은 제가 먼저 말을 꺼내고 싶었어요.
Actually, I wanted to bring it up first.
examples: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요.
Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.
Opens bad news with a softer frame.
nuance: 사실은 does not mean every sentence is a dramatic confession. It often simply prepares the listener for background or a correction.
mistakes: Using 사실은 and then giving information the listener already knows very well. 잖아요 may fit better for shared information.
Translating 'actually' into 사실은 in every English sentence; sometimes 그런데 or 아니면 no marker is more natural.

usage: The meeting time is short, you know.
Can sound pointed depending on tone.
examples: 팀장님도 지금 바쁘시잖아요.
The team lead is busy now too, you know.
Uses shared context to justify a suggestion.
nuance: 잖아요 is for shared information. For new background, use -거든요 instead.
mistakes: Using 잖아요 to announce new information. That can sound like 'You should have known this.'
Using it in formal public speech. It is conversational.

usage: Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
That cafe has a nice atmosphere, you see.
Reason for liking or choosing the cafe.
examples: 오늘은 먼저 시작해 주세요. 제가 조금 늦거든요.
Please start first today. I am running a little late, you see.
Explains a request with new background.
nuance: 거든요 gives new background. It is softer than just dropping a reason, but it can sound defensive if the tone is too clipped.
mistakes: Using 거든요 for something everyone already knows. 잖아요 is usually better for shared information.
Treating it as a full replacement for because. It carries conversational background, not just logic.

english: though; you see; soft trailing ending
usage: I am a little busy right now, though.
The materials are not finished yet, though.
Bad news without sounding too blunt.
examples: 그 의견도 좋은데요, 시간이 조금 부족해요.
That opinion is good too, but we are a little short on time.
Soft contrast before disagreement.
nuance: 는데요 is not only 'but'. It often sets up background and hands the next move to the listener.
mistakes: Using 는데요 as a random polite ending in every sentence.
Forgetting the adjective form: 바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요.

usage: Slides or handouts for a presentation.
examples: 회의 전에 자료를 보내 줄게요.
I will send the materials before the meeting.
Practical work or study-group sentence.
nuance: 자료 can mean data, but in daily work and study talk it often means the file, handout, or slide deck someone needs.
mistakes: Using 정보 for every kind of material. 정보 is information; 자료 is often the actual file or reference material.
Confusing 자료 with 의견. 의견 means opinion.

usage: Useful before a proposal or disagreement.
A soft way to introduce context.
examples: 제가 먼저 배경을 설명할게요.
I will explain the background first.
Keeps the conversation organized.
nuance: 배경 is broader than 이유. 이유 is the reason; 배경 is the surrounding context that makes the reason understandable.
mistakes: Using 이유 when the listener needs a fuller context. 배경 may sound more natural.
Overusing 배경 in very casual chat where 그냥 왜냐하면 is enough.

usage: when the other person does not know
Important for choosing 거든요 instead of 잖아요.
to consider the other person's feelings
examples: 상대방이 처음 듣는 내용이면 거든요가 더 자연스러워요.
If the other person is hearing it for the first time, 거든요 is more natural.
Explains the usage boundary.
nuance: 상대방 is neutral. It is not necessarily an opponent; it can simply mean the other person in the interaction.
mistakes: Thinking 상대방 always means an enemy or opponent. In conversation study, it usually means the listener.
Ignoring what the 상대방 already knows when choosing 잖아요 or 거든요.

examples: 그 의견에는 부드럽게 반대하는 게 좋아요.
It is better to disagree with that opinion gently.
Connects tone with disagreement.
nuance: 부드럽게 is about manner or tone. It does not automatically make the content polite if the sentence itself is too direct.
mistakes: Calling every polite sentence 부드럽게. The sentence must actually soften the delivery.
Forgetting that tone and grammar work together in Korean.

usage: Starting a topic before someone else does.
examples: 자료가 늦어진 이야기는 제가 먼저 말을 꺼낼게요.
I will bring up the delayed materials first.
A real meeting or team-project sentence.
nuance: 말을 꺼내다 is about starting a topic, not physically taking words out. It often implies a little hesitation or tact.
mistakes: Reading 말 as an unrelated animal noun. In this phrase, 말 means words or speech.
Using 말하다 when the point is initiating a difficult topic. 말을 꺼내다 is more precise.

usage: when I went and saw / tried going
examples: 그 식당에 가 보니까 생각보다 조용하더라고요.
When I tried going to that restaurant, it was quieter than I expected.
Experience leads to a firsthand observation.
nuance: 보니까 is evidence-based. It sounds odd if you did not actually see, try, or check the thing.
mistakes: Using 보니까 for pure hearsay. If someone only told you, use a reported-speech form instead.
Forgetting the try/check meaning in 가 보다 or 확인해 보다.

usage: It was better than I expected.
There were a lot of people, I noticed.
examples: 요즘은 분위기가 많이 달라졌더라고요.
These days, the atmosphere has changed a lot, I noticed.
Reports a noticed change.
nuance: 더라고요 is not just past tense. It carries the speaker's evidence and realization.
mistakes: Using 더라고요 for something you only heard from someone else.
Using it for your own planned action as if you observed yourself from outside.

english: I observed X, and then Y happened
usage: it was quiet at first, and then...
Observed repeated action followed by result.
examples: 처음에는 조용하더니 금방 사람이 많아졌어요.
It was quiet at first, and then there were quickly more people.
A direct observed change.
nuance: Plain -더니 has an eyewitness feel. For your own action causing a result, -았/었더니 is usually the safer form.
mistakes: Saying 내가 가더니 for your own neutral action. Use 갔더니 when your own action led to a result.
Using -더니 when there is no change or result after the first observation.

usage: Often used with 나오다 or 끝나다.
examples: 음식이 생각보다 빨리 나오더라고요.
The food came out faster than expected, I noticed.
Expectation plus firsthand observation.
nuance: 생각보다 naturally pairs with 더라고요 because both talk about what you found after experience.
mistakes: Using 생각보다 without saying what was different from expectation.
Confusing 생각보다 with 그냥 생각. 생각보다 is a comparison phrase.

examples: 처음에는 조용하더니 금방 붐볐어요.
It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded.
Natural setup for an observed change.
nuance: 처음에는 points to the first stage. It needs a later stage to feel complete.
mistakes: Using 처음에는 without showing what changed afterward.
Confusing 처음에는 with 처음으로, which means 'for the first time.'

usage: There used to be few people.
examples: 예전에는 조용했는데 요즘은 사람이 많더라고요.
It used to be quiet, but these days there are many people, I noticed.
Before-now contrast.
nuance: 예전에는 is broader than 어제 or 지난주. It points to an earlier period, not one exact moment.
mistakes: Using 예전에는 for a single recent event when 어제 or 지난번 is clearer.
Forgetting the contrast when using 예전에는 in a change sentence.

usage: These days there are many people.
The atmosphere has changed these days.
examples: 요즘은 손님이 많이 늘었더라고요.
These days, the number of customers has increased a lot, I noticed.
Current observation after change.
nuance: 요즘은 is not just today. It means the recent/current period.
mistakes: Using 요즘은 for one event that happened only today.
Forgetting that 요즘은 often invites a contrast with before.

english: to come to know; to find out
usage: to come to know through experience
examples: 직접 가 보니까 왜 유명한지 알게 됐어요.
After going there myself, I found out why it is famous.
Realization after firsthand experience.
nuance: 알게 되다 emphasizes the process of finding out. 알다 simply states that you know.
mistakes: Using 알게 되다 when you already knew the fact all along.
Forgetting that it often pairs with a discovery trigger like 보니까, 듣고 나서, or 경험하면서.

examples: 일주일 동안 분위기가 어떻게 변하는지 관찰했어요.
I observed how the atmosphere changed over a week.
Careful observation of change.
nuance: 관찰하다 is useful for deliberate observation. For a casual visit, 가 보니까 or 보니까 often sounds more natural.
mistakes: Using 관찰하다 for every casual noticing. It can sound too deliberate or academic.
Forgetting that 더라고요 still needs firsthand evidence, even if the verb 관찰하다 is not used.

examples: 처음에는 조용하더니 금방 붐비더라고요.
It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded, I noticed.
A natural restaurant or event observation.
nuance: 붐비다 describes the place or route becoming crowded. 사람이 많다 describes the number of people more directly.
mistakes: Using 붐비다 for one person being busy. For a busy person, use 바쁘다.
Forgetting that 붐비다 usually needs a place or traffic-like subject.

usage: They said we will take it on Friday.
They said they are busy today.
examples: 선생님이 시험은 금요일에 본다고 하셨어요.
The teacher said the exam is on Friday.
Respectful reporting with 하셨어요.
nuance: 다고 했어요 reports a statement, not a question or command. Match the inner ending to the sentence type.
mistakes: Using -다고 for questions. A reported question needs -냐고.
Forgetting present action-verb forms like 간다고 and 먹는다고.

usage: They asked what time we are meeting.
They asked whether I submitted the homework.
examples: 친구가 시험이 언제냐고 물어봤어요.
My friend asked when the exam is.
Question content stays question-marked with -냐고.
nuance: 냐고 is for reported questions. Do not switch to -다고 just because the whole sentence now ends like a statement.
mistakes: Saying 언제 온다고 물어봤어요 when you mean 'asked when they are coming'. Use 언제 오냐고 물어봤어요.
Overusing the formal textbook -느냐고 in everyday conversation when -냐고 is natural.

usage: Do you know when the exam is?
Please check what time we are meeting.
examples: 선생님이 시험이 언제인지도 말씀하셨어요?
Did the teacher also say when the exam is?
The question 'when is the exam?' sits inside a larger question.
nuance: 는지 is not reported speech by itself. It embeds a question so verbs like 알다, 모르다, 확인하다, and 궁금하다 can use it.
mistakes: Using -냐고 when no one asked a question. If you just do not know the answer, use -는지.
Using -는지 for a direct quote instead of an embedded question.

usage: They told us to submit the homework.
They said to check the message.
examples: 선생님이 내일까지 숙제를 제출하라고 하셨어요.
The teacher told us to submit the homework by tomorrow.
Classroom instruction being passed along.
nuance: 라고 하다 for instructions is separate from noun +(이)라고 하다, as in 학생이라고 했어요.
mistakes: Using -다고 하다 for commands: 제출한다고 하셨어요 means 'said they will submit', not 'told us to submit'.
Confusing reported command -(으)라고 with noun quote -(이)라고.

usage: They say they are coming tomorrow.
They say they are busy today.
examples: 선생님이 시험은 금요일에 본대요.
The teacher says the exam is on Friday.
Spoken version of 본다고 해요.
nuance: 대요 is common, but first learn what it expands from so you do not mix statements with questions.
mistakes: Using 대요 for reported questions. Questions contract to 냬요 in casual speech.
Forgetting the source of the information when using 대요.

english: to ask; to ask and find out
usage: to ask what time it is
examples: 친구가 몇 시에 만나냐고 물어봤어요.
My friend asked what time we are meeting.
Reported question with the everyday verb 물어보다.
nuance: 묻다 is the dictionary/base verb. 물어보다 is often the natural spoken choice for asking someone.
mistakes: Using 묻다 forms mechanically when 물어보다 sounds more natural in conversation.
Forgetting the person marker: 친구한테 물어봤어요 or 선생님께 물어봤어요.

examples: 못 들었으면 다시 말해 달라고 해요.
If you did not hear it, ask them to say it again.
Useful repair phrase in reported speech practice.
nuance: 다시 말하다 is not just the adverb 다시. It is a practical repair phrase when reported information is unclear.
mistakes: Treating 다시 말하다 as only the word 다시. The useful chunk is the whole phrase.
Using it when you need 확인하다 instead: 다시 말하다 repeats; 확인하다 checks.

usage: to check the notice posted today
examples: 어제 올라온 공지를 다시 확인했어요.
I checked the notice posted yesterday again.
Unpacks a real portal-notice phrase.
nuance: 올라온 is not a separate full sentence here. It sits before 공지 and tells you which notice.
mistakes: Reading 올라온 as a separate sentence and losing the final noun 공지.
Confusing 올라온 공지 with 올라갈 공지. 올라온 is already posted; 올라갈 is going to be posted.

usage: to review the report to submit
examples: 내일 제출할 보고서를 다시 검토했어요.
I reviewed the report I will submit tomorrow again.
Shows future noun modification in a real task.
nuance: 제출할 points forward. It differs from 제출한 보고서, a report that was already submitted.
mistakes: Reading 제출할 as a standalone future sentence instead of a modifier for 보고서.
Confusing 제출할 보고서 with 제출한 보고서.

english: to be written; to be used
usage: the expression used/written in the notice
a word that is often used
examples: 공지에 쓰인 표현이 조금 어려웠어요.
The expression used in the notice was a little difficult.
Focuses on the expression, not the writer.
nuance: 쓰이다 focuses on the written/used item. 쓰다 focuses on the person writing or using it.
mistakes: Using 쓰다 when the sentence subject is the expression or word itself. 공지에 쓰인 표현 is the natural phrase.
Forgetting that 쓰이다 can mean both 'be written' and 'be used.'

english: to have no choice but to
usage: I have no choice but to work late.
I have no choice but to check again.
examples: 마감이 오늘이라서 이 방법을 선택할 수밖에 없어요.
The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to choose this method.
No-choice situation plus reason.
nuance: 수밖에 없다 is resignation to the only remaining option, not inability.
mistakes: Using 할 수 없어요 when you mean 'I have no choice but to do it.' 할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it.
Writing 수 밖에 with a space in this fixed expression. Use 수밖에.

usage: There is no way we would give up now.
There is no way the data is wrong.
examples: 그 사람이 마감을 잊었을 리가 없어요.
There is no way that person forgot the deadline.
Strong logical disbelief.
nuance: 리가 없다 carries confidence or emotional conviction. It is not a neutral maybe-not.
mistakes: Using 방법이 없다 for 'there is no way that.' 방법이 없다 means there is no method.
Using 리가 없다 when you only mean a soft guess. For uncertainty, use -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 or 아마 아닐 거예요.

english: to be only; to be nothing but
usage: The only thing left is this method.
examples: 결국 우리가 할 수 있는 건 수정뿐이에요.
In the end, all we can do is revise it.
Limits the choice to one remaining action.
nuance: 뿐이다 closes the scope. It differs from 뿐만 아니라, which opens the sentence to an additional point.
mistakes: Confusing 뿐이다 with 뿐만 아니라. 뿐이다 means only; 뿐만 아니라 means not only but also.
Using 만 when the whole action, not just a noun, needs limiting.

usage: They are probably still in a meeting.
examples: 그분은 아직 회사에 있을걸요.
They are probably still at the office.
Careful workplace guess.
nuance: 걸요 is softer than a plain statement, but it is not as open-ended as 글쎄요. The speaker still has a hunch.
mistakes: Using 걸요 for a wish. For wishes, use -(으)면 좋겠어요.
Confusing sentence-final -걸요 with regret -ㄹ걸 그랬어요.

english: I hope; it would be good if...
usage: I hope the reply comes quickly.
It would be good to leave a message.
examples: 확실하지 않으면 먼저 물어보면 좋겠어요.
If you are not sure, it would be good to ask first.
Careful advice.
nuance: 좋겠어요 is useful when you want to express a hope or suggestion without sounding like an order.
mistakes: Using 좋겠어요 as plain 'I like it.' For liking, use 좋아요.
Using it when you need a firm instruction.

usage: if I were the person in charge
examples: 혹시 이미 퇴근했다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
If they already left work, it would be good to leave a message.
Hypothetical plus gentle solution.
nuance: 다면 often feels more hypothetical or careful than plain -(으)면.
mistakes: Using 다면 for every real condition. Plain -(으)면 is often enough for simple real-world conditions.
Forgetting noun form N이라면.

usage: I think it feels a bit burdensome.
examples: 제 생각에는 먼저 물어보는 게 좋을 것 같아요.
In my opinion, I think it would be good to ask first.
Careful opinion instead of a blunt order.
nuance: 것 같아요 is not the same as 같다 meaning 'same.' Here it softens the whole statement.
mistakes: Linking 것 같아요 to 같다 as 'same' and missing the hedge meaning.
Keeping a full English-style clause before it. Korean turns the idea into a modifier before 것.

english: will; must be; I see (inference/volition marker)
examples: 제가 조심스럽게 물어보겠습니다.
I will ask carefully.
Formal intention.
nuance: 겠 is not one English word. It can be intention, inference, or a set response depending on context.
mistakes: Treating every 겠 as future tense only.
Using 겠어요 too strongly when 것 같아요 would be a softer guess.

examples: 확실하지 않으니까 조심스럽게 물어볼게요.
Since I am not sure, I will ask carefully.
Careful action because the information is uncertain.
nuance: 조심스럽게 is about tone and risk. It is not just physical carefulness.
mistakes: Using it as a noun. It is an adverb: 조심스럽게 말해요.
Thinking grammar alone creates softness. Word choice and tone also matter.

usage: I gave a gift to a friend.
I also gave a gift to the teacher.
께 is honorific; 도 means also.
examples: 작은 선물이라도 준비하면 좋겠어요.
It would be good to prepare at least a small gift.
이라도 gives the sense of at least.
nuance: 선물 can be the thing given, received, bought, or prepared. In this chapter, focus on the particle around the person and the particle attached to 선물 itself.
mistakes: Using 에게 with objects instead of people. Say 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, not 선물에게.
Forgetting that 도 and 만 can replace 을/를: 선물도 줬어요, 선물만 샀어요.

usage: I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.
있다 marks the presence of the allergy.
examples: 고기는 싫어서 안 먹는 게 아니라 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요.
It is not that I avoid meat because I dislike it; I cannot eat it because of an allergy.
Contrasts 안 먹다 with 못 먹다.
nuance: 알레르기 gives a concrete outside reason. In Korean this often makes 못 sound appropriate because the limit is physical or medical, not a preference.
mistakes: Saying 안 먹어요 when the reason is a medical restriction and you need 못 먹어요.
Using 알레르기 like an adjective. Say 알레르기가 있어요 or 우유 알레르기가 있어요.

usage: There are four people in my family.
Polite family introduction to someone outside the family.
Humble 우리 with respectful family noun 부모님.
examples: 회사 동료에게는 '저희 가족은 네 명이에요'라고 말해요.
To a coworker, say 'There are four people in my family.'
저희 fits polite outside-the-family introductions.
nuance: 저희 is not colder than 우리; it is socially careful. Use it when the listener is outside your group and the situation is polite. Use 우리 with close friends, family, and many natural everyday phrases like 우리 엄마.
mistakes: Using 제 가족은 too mechanically. It is possible, but 저희 가족은 sounds more natural in polite introductions.
Using 저희 for the listener's family. 저희 lowers your own side, not the other person's side.
Forgetting that 저희 pairs naturally with 가족 and 부모님 in formal or semi-formal introductions.

usage: 하루 세 번, 식후에 드셔야 해요.
You have to take it three times a day after meals.
examples: 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드세요.
Take the medicine three times a day after meals.
약 + 식후 + 하루 세 번 is the core pharmacy frame.
nuance: 식후 is concise and label-like. In casual speech you can also say 밥 먹고, but at a clinic or pharmacy 식후 is the expected word. 식후 usually pairs with 에 or a time amount: 식후에, 식후 30분.
mistakes: Using 식후 for any after-action meaning. It specifically means after meals.
Confusing 식후 with 식전. 식후 is after meals; 식전 is before meals.
Forgetting 에 in speech: 식후에 드세요 is smoother than just 식후 드세요.

usage: I came to see a studio apartment.
Is the maintenance fee separate for this studio?
examples: 이 원룸은 보증금 500만 원에 월세 70만 원이에요.
This studio has a 5 million won deposit and 700,000 won monthly rent.
Common listing-price structure.
nuance: 원룸 literally comes from 'one room', but in Korean it is a housing category, not just any one room. It usually means a small self-contained studio with a bathroom and kitchenette.
mistakes: Translating every 'room' as 원룸. 방 is a room; 원룸 is a studio apartment.
Forgetting that 원룸 listings are usually quoted with both 보증금 and 월세.
Assuming 관리비 is always included. Always ask 관리비는 따로예요?

usage: I went to a real-estate office to see a studio.
I checked the contract at the real-estate office.
examples: 집을 구하기 위해 부동산에 갔어요.
I went to a real-estate office to find a place.
-기 위해 gives the planned purpose.
nuance: When Koreans say 부동산에 가요, they usually mean the neighborhood office, not an abstract real-estate market. For the person, say 공인중개사 or 중개사.
mistakes: Thinking 부동산 only means property. In conversation it often means the real-estate office.
Calling the agent 부동산 사람 too vaguely when 공인중개사 or 중개사 is clearer.
Forgetting 에/에서: 부동산에 가다, 부동산에서 계약하다.

usage: Is it jeonse or monthly rent?
The jeonse deposit is too expensive.
전세 still revolves around a deposit.
examples: 저는 전세보다 월세 원룸을 찾고 있어요.
I am looking for a monthly-rent studio rather than jeonse.
Useful for telling an agent your housing type.
nuance: 전세 is not simply 'deposit'. The deposit itself is 보증금; 전세 is the lease type built around a very large deposit.
mistakes: Using 전세 when you mean any deposit. The deposit is 보증금.
Assuming 월세 has no deposit. 월세 often also has 보증금.
Translating 전세 as monthly rent. Monthly rent is 월세.

usage: Check the contract and keep it prepared.
The deposit is written in the contract.
examples: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 다시 확인해야 해요.
Before moving, you have to check the contract again.
Practical pre-move task.
nuance: 계약서 is the document, while 계약하다 is the action of making/signing the contract. Do not blur them when asking questions.
mistakes: Saying 계약해요 when you mean the paper itself. The paper is 계약서.
Not checking whether 관리비 and options are included before signing.
Forgetting the object marker: 계약서를 확인하다.

usage: Can I sign the contract today?
Possibility question with ㄹ 수 있어요.
Before signing, check the maintenance fee.
examples: 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있어요.
If you like it, you can sign the contract today.
Real-estate agent line.
nuance: 계약하다 is broader than housing, but in this chapter it should stay tied to real-estate contracts. 계약서를 확인하다 happens before 계약하다.
mistakes: Using 예약하다 for signing a lease. 예약하다 is reserve/book; 계약하다 is contract.
Forgetting that 계약하다 is the action and 계약서 is the document.
Saying 계약을 쓰다 is possible in some contexts, but 계약하다 is the safe learner verb.

usage: Is internet included in the maintenance fee?
The water bill is included in the maintenance fee.
examples: 인터넷이 포함돼 있으면 바로 계약할 수 있어요.
If internet is included, I can sign right away.
Condition tied to a housing decision.
nuance: 포함되다 focuses on what is included in a price or category. Do not use it like English 'include' with the fee as active subject unless you restructure the sentence.
mistakes: Saying 관리비가 인터넷을 포함해요 too literally. The natural housing question is 인터넷이 관리비에 포함돼 있어요?
Forgetting 에 after 관리비: 관리비에 포함되다.
Confusing 포함되다 with 필요하다. 포함되다 is about inclusion, not need.

usage: You have to pay the electricity bill separately.
examples: 관리비가 따로면 월세가 더 비싸게 느껴져요.
If the maintenance fee is separate, the monthly rent feels more expensive.
Condition that changes the decision.
nuance: 따로 is not only about money, but housing learners need it for separate fees and separate payments.
mistakes: Asking only 월세가 얼마예요? and forgetting 관리비는 따로예요?
Using 따로 as a noun. It works as an adverb or predicate with 이다: 따로 내요, 따로예요.
Missing the hidden total cost when 관리비 or utilities are 따로.

usage: 맞다 is about size or correctness, not style.
examples: 사이즈가 조금 커서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
The size is a little big, so could you show me one size smaller too?
Combines size judgment with a polite staff request.
nuance: 사이즈 is the size label or fit. Use 맞다 for whether it fits, and 어울리다 for whether it looks good on someone.
mistakes: Using 어울리다 for size. 사이즈가 맞아요 means it fits; 잘 어울려요 means it suits you.
Asking only 이거 있어요? when you need a size. Say 다른 사이즈 있어요?
Forgetting that shop staff may ask 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? to mean what size would you like?

usage: 큰 modifies 거 through the adjective modifier form.
작은 is the modifier form of 작다.
examples: 한 치수 작은 것도 입어 봐도 돼요?
May I try on one size smaller too?
Natural fitting-room sentence.
nuance: 사이즈 is the everyday label; 치수 is the size measurement or one-step comparison used in 한 치수 큰/작은.
mistakes: Saying 더 작은 사이즈 only every time. 한 치수 작은 거 is compact and natural in clothing stores.
Confusing 치수 with 가격. 치수 is about size or measurement, not price.
Forgetting the modifier: 한 치수 작아요 describes a size, but 한 치수 작은 거 asks for the item.

usage: The fitting room is on the right.
examples: 이 셔츠 입어 보고 싶은데 피팅룸이 어디예요?
I want to try on this shirt. Where is the fitting room?
Connects trying on with store navigation.
nuance: 피팅룸 is used in many stores, but 탈의실 also means changing room. For clothing shopping, 피팅룸 is natural and easy to understand.
mistakes: Calling staff with 피팅룸? alone. Make it a full question: 피팅룸이 어디예요?
Using 입다 without try-on meaning. 입어 봐도 돼요? asks permission to try it on.
Assuming every shop allows try-ons; ask first for cosmetics, innerwear, sale items, or delicate clothing.

examples: 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.
Connects interview clothing with comparison and appearance.
nuance: 단정하다 means neat, orderly, and socially appropriate. It is not the same as stylish or trendy; it is often safer for interviews, school, and work.
mistakes: Using 예쁘다 for every clothing compliment. 예쁘다 is pretty; 단정하다 is neat and appropriate.
Saying 단정 옷. Use the modifier form: 단정한 옷.
Confusing 단정하다 with 깨끗하다. 깨끗하다 is clean; 단정하다 is presentable and orderly.

usage: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal.
Please give us one more serving.
examples: 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나 주세요.
Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal and one bowl of rice.
Combines a serving counter and a rice order.
nuance: 명 counts people; 인분 counts portions. 두 명 왔어요 says two people came, but 두 인분 주세요 orders two servings.
mistakes: Using 명 to order food. Say 삼겹살 두 인분, not 삼겹살 두 명.
Forgetting that some restaurants have a minimum order such as 2인분.
Treating 인분 as exactly the eater count. People can order more or fewer servings than the number of people.

usage: Please give me one bowl of rice.
We will add a bowl of rice.
Common after ordering meat or stew.
examples: 양념이 매워서 공기밥을 같이 먹어요.
The seasoning is spicy, so I eat it with a bowl of rice.
Reason plus food pairing.
nuance: 밥 can mean cooked rice or a meal. 공기밥 is the restaurant item, a separate bowl of rice.
mistakes: Ordering 밥 vaguely when the menu item is 공기밥.
Confusing 공기밥 with 볶음밥. 공기밥 is plain rice; 볶음밥 is fried rice.
Forgetting the counter: 공기밥 하나/두 개 is common.

usage: Please give us a little more side dishes.
examples: 밑반찬이 부족하니까 더 주세요.
The side dishes are not enough, so please give us more.
Uses -니까 before a request.
nuance: 밑반찬 is not the main dish. It refers to small supporting dishes such as kimchi, vegetables, or pickles served with the meal.
mistakes: Calling every Korean side dish 밑반찬 in every context. On a menu, 반찬 or 사이드 may also appear.
Forgetting 좀 in refill requests. 밑반찬 좀 더 주세요 sounds softer.
Assuming refills are always unlimited; most ordinary restaurants refill, but special side dishes may not be free.

examples: 고기가 익었으니까 이제 잘라 주세요.
The meat is cooked now, so please cut it.
-니까 gives the reason for the request.
nuance: 익다 is intransitive: 고기가 익어요. 익히다 is transitive: 고기를 익혀요, to cook something through.
mistakes: Saying 고기를 익어요. Use 고기가 익어요 because the meat becomes cooked.
Confusing 익다 with 굽다. 굽다 is the cooking action; 익다 is the result.
Using 익다 only for fruit. It also works for meat, rice, and other food becoming cooked.

usage: Please give me just a little ssamjang.
Useful if the sauce is strong or salty.
The ssamjang is a bit salty.
examples: 쌈장이 짜니까 조금만 넣으세요.
The ssamjang is salty, so put in only a little.
Reason plus advice.
nuance: 쌈장 is not the same as 고추장. It is a mixed paste commonly used for wraps with grilled meat.
mistakes: Calling every red sauce 고추장. 쌈장 is a specific wrap sauce.
Using too much without tasting; 쌈장 can be salty.
Forgetting that 쌈장 often goes with 상추, 마늘, and grilled meat.

usage: Have you watched this drama before?
What drama are you watching these days?
examples: 친구가 이 드라마 재미있다고 했어요.
My friend said this drama is fun.
Reported recommendation.
nuance: 드라마 usually means a scripted series, not a one-off movie. 영화 is movie; 예능 is variety show.
mistakes: Using 영화 for every streamed show. A series is usually 드라마.
Forgetting 보다: 드라마를 봐요, not 드라마를 들어요.
Using 본 적 있어요 for something you watched yesterday with a time. Use 봤어요 for a dated event.

examples: 배우도 좋지만 댓글이 더 재미있거든요.
The actor is good too, but the comments are more fun, you know.
A reason/background sentence for online content.
nuance: 댓글 is online. For a spoken comment or opinion, 말 or 의견 may fit better.
mistakes: Saying 댓글을 쓰다 is understandable, but 댓글을 달다 is the standard collocation.
Using 코멘트 for ordinary social media comments. 댓글 is the everyday word.
Forgetting subject/object particles: 댓글이 재미있어요, 댓글을 달아요.

usage: I shared it with a friend.
examples: 재미있어서 친구한테 영상을 공유했어요.
It was fun, so I shared the video with a friend.
Reason plus digital action.
nuance: 공유하다 is broader than sending. 보내다 is to send; 공유하다 emphasizes making content available or passing it along.
mistakes: Using 나누다 for social media sharing. Use 공유하다 for links, videos, and files.
Forgetting the object: 영상을 공유했어요, 링크를 공유했어요.
Mixing 공유하다 with 저장하다. Sharing is not saving.

examples: 친구가 자막이 좋다고 했어요.
My friend said the subtitles are good.
Reported opinion.
nuance: 자막 can mean subtitles for translation or captions on video. In streaming apps, 자막 설정 is subtitle settings.
mistakes: Confusing 자막 with 제목. 자막 is subtitles; 제목 is a title.
Saying 자막을 봐요 when you mean the subtitles show on screen. Use 자막이 나와요.
Forgetting that 자막 takes 이/가 when it appears: 자막이 안 나와요.

examples: 영상이 계속 끊기는데요.
The video keeps cutting out, though.
-는데요 softly raises the problem.
nuance: 끊기다 is passive/intransitive: the video or connection cuts out. 끊다 is what someone actively cuts or ends.
mistakes: Using 끊다 for a video problem. Say 영상이 끊겨요, not 영상을 끊어요.
Confusing 끊기다 with 느리다. 느리다 is slow; 끊기다 is stopping/cutting out.
Forgetting the subject: 영상이 끊겨요, 와이파이가 끊겨요.

usage: Did you see that idol's stage?
examples: 친구가 그 아이돌 무대가 대박이라고 했어요.
My friend said that idol's stage was amazing.
Reported fan reaction.
nuance: 아이돌 can refer to a solo idol or group member. For the whole group, 그룹 or 아이돌 그룹 is clearer.
mistakes: Using 가수 for every K-pop idol. 가수 is singer; 아이돌 includes the fandom/performance context.
Forgetting that borrowed words still take Korean particles: 아이돌이, 아이돌을, 아이돌한테.
Using formal fan slang before you understand the fandom context.

examples: 영상이 계속 끊기면 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보세요.
If the video keeps cutting out, try reconnecting the Wi-Fi.
Problem plus suggested action.
nuance: 연결하다 is active: you connect something. 연결되다 means something is connected.
mistakes: Using 연결하다 when the subject is the Wi-Fi itself. 와이파이가 연결됐어요 is natural for 'the Wi-Fi is connected.'
Confusing 연결하다 with 공유하다. 연결하다 connects; 공유하다 shares content.
Forgetting 을/를 for what you connect: 와이파이를 연결해요.

usage: Honorific verb ending for the professor.
examples: 중간고사 전에 교수님께 질문하기로 했어요.
I decided to ask the professor before the midterm.
Decision plus school context.
nuance: Use 선생님 for school teachers or language teachers, and 교수님 for university professors.
mistakes: Calling a university professor 선생님 is understandable, but 교수님 is more natural.
Using 교수 without 님 when addressing or referring respectfully.
Using 한테 in formal writing to a professor; 께 is more respectful.

examples: 이번 학기 동안 매일 한국어를 공부하기로 했어요.
I decided to study Korean every day during this semester.
학기 plus 동안.
nuance: 학기 is an academic term; 방학 is vacation/break between terms.
mistakes: Using 학기 for a single class period. A class period is 수업 or 시간.
Confusing 학기 with 학년. 학기 is semester; 학년 is grade/year.
Adding 에 before 동안: say 한 학기 동안, not 한 학기에 동안.

examples: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요.
We have to finish the presentation assignment before the midterm.
Exam deadline plus obligation.
nuance: 중간 means middle; 고사 is exam. In daily student talk, 시험 is more general, while 중간고사 is specifically the midterm.
mistakes: Using 중간고사 for every test. Use 시험 for general exams.
Confusing 중간고사 with 기말고사. Midterm comes in the middle; final comes at the end.
Forgetting the timing phrase: 중간고사 전에, 중간고사 동안, 중간고사 끝나고.

usage: 보다 is used for taking exams.
examples: 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해 매일 공부해야 해요.
I have to study every day in order to get a good grade on the final exam.
Purpose plus obligation.
nuance: 기말 means the end of the term. 기말고사 is final exam; 중간고사 is midterm exam.
mistakes: Using 기말고사 before the middle of the semester. That is 중간고사.
Saying 시험을 치다/보다 both work for taking an exam; 시험을 만들다 does not mean take an exam.
Using 에 with 기말고사 when the sentence is about results. Say 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받다.

examples: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내기로 했어요.
We decided to finish the presentation assignment before the midterm.
Decision plus assignment.
nuance: 숙제 is homework, often younger-school or daily work. 과제 sounds more academic and can include reports, presentations, and projects.
mistakes: Using 숙제 for every university assignment. 과제 is often more natural.
Forgetting the object marker when needed: 과제를 끝내요.
Confusing 과제 with 문제. 문제 is a question/problem; 과제 is an assigned task.

usage: Natural question when checking a route.
으로 marks the line you change to.
examples: 서울역에 가려면 몇 호선으로 갈아타요?
Which line do I transfer to if I want to get to Seoul Station?
Route question plus transfer.
nuance: 호선 is for subway line labels, not for bus routes. Say 2호선 for Line 2, but 버스 노선 for a bus route.
mistakes: Saying 2노선 for Line 2. Subway lines use 호선: 2호선.
Using 호선 for bus routes. Use 노선 for buses.
Forgetting 으로/로 with transfers: 1호선으로 갈아타세요.

english: to book or buy a ticket in advance
usage: 표 is the object; 예매하다 is the booking action.
I booked it in the app.
에서 marks where the booking action happened.
examples: 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 해요.
I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan.
Natural ticket-counter or app sentence.
nuance: 예매하다 is ticket-centered and usually means the seat or ticket is secured before departure or showtime. 예약하다 is broader and can mean reserving a restaurant, hotel, appointment, or service.
mistakes: Using 예약하다 for every ticket situation. It may be understood, but KTX/movie/concert tickets naturally use 예매하다.
Forgetting the object: 표를 예매하다, not just KTX를 예매하다 when you mean the ticket.
Confusing 예매하다 with 사다. 사다 is buy in general; 예매하다 adds advance booking.

examples: 부산 가는 표는 편도로 예매할게요.
I will book the ticket to Busan one-way.
으로/로 marks ticket type here.
nuance: 편도 is the opposite of 왕복. It answers the ticket type question, not the destination question.
mistakes: Saying 한쪽 for a one-way ticket. Use 편도.
Confusing 편도 with 편의점. They only sound partly similar.
Forgetting the counter when buying: 편도 한 장 주세요.

examples: 서울에서 부산까지 왕복으로 예매했어요.
I booked a round trip from Seoul to Busan.
Useful when both directions are fixed.
nuance: 왕복 is the ticket-plan pair of 편도. The question 편도예요, 왕복이에요? is a normal ticket-counter question.
mistakes: Using 돌아오는 표 when the counter simply asks ticket type. 왕복 is the compact ticket word.
Confusing 왕복 with 반복. 반복 means repetition.
Buying 왕복 when your return time is not fixed can be inconvenient; 편도 may be safer.

english: sold out for tickets or seats
examples: KTX 표가 매진이면 다음 기차로 예매하세요.
If the KTX tickets are sold out, book the next train.
매진 plus V면 creates the fallback plan.
nuance: 매진 is for tickets and seats. 품절 is for products on a shelf or in an online store.
mistakes: Using 품절 for train tickets. Say 매진.
Saying 매진하다 for the customer's action. The ticket is 매진되다 or 매진이에요.
Forgetting that 매진 often needs a fallback sentence: 매진이면 다음 기차로 가요.

examples: 버스 지연 때문에 약속에 늦었어요.
I was late to the appointment because of a bus delay.
N 때문에 names the cause.
nuance: 지연 sounds more official than 늦다. Use 늦다 for a person being late and 지연 for a service, schedule, or system delay.
mistakes: Saying 사람이 지연됐어요 for a person. Say 사람이 늦었어요.
Using 늦다 when the service delay is the topic. For announcements, 지연되다 is more natural.
Adding a particle before 때문에: say 버스 지연 때문에, not 버스 지연이 때문에.

usage: The interval between buses or trains is long.
examples: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.
Connects route information to a transport choice.
nuance: 배차 간격 is not the travel time. It is the gap between one bus or train and the next one.
mistakes: Confusing 배차 간격 with 소요 시간. 소요 시간 is how long the trip takes.
Using it for one delayed vehicle. 지연 is delay; 배차 간격 is the normal interval.
Forgetting 이/가 with the measured interval: 배차 간격이 길어요.

usage: to go to the ticket counter
to book at the ticket counter
에서 marks where the booking happens.
examples: KTX 표 예매하러 매표소에 가요.
I am going to the ticket counter to book a KTX ticket.
Purpose plus destination.
nuance: 매표소 is the selling place for tickets. 표 is the ticket itself, and 예매하다 is the booking action.
mistakes: Confusing 매표소 with 표. 매표소 is the place; 표 is the ticket.
Using 에서 when only naming the destination. Say 매표소에 가요, but 매표소에서 예매해요.
Calling every service desk 매표소. It is specifically for ticket sales.

usage: If we are the same age, can we speak casually?
Age does not automatically remove politeness; you still check.
examples: 나이가 비슷하면 동갑이라고 말해도 돼요?
If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?
Socially careful age question.
nuance: 동갑 is useful because Korean relationships often adjust around age. Still, being 동갑 does not mean you immediately use 반말; closeness and setting matter too.
mistakes: Assuming 동갑 means you can use 반말 immediately. Ask or wait for the other person to suggest it.
Using 친구 only because someone is the same age. 친구 implies relationship, not just age.
Forgetting final consonant pronunciation: 동갑 sounds like dong-gap, with the final ㅂ pronounced clearly before a vowel.

usage: to decide on a title/form of address
Common after age or role is known.
examples: 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
At first, people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.
Polite title choice.
nuance: 호칭 is not just a word choice; it signals age, role, closeness, and respect. When unsure, asking 어떤 호칭을 쓰면 될까요? is safer than guessing too casually.
mistakes: Calling an older coworker by first name without checking. Use a title or ask first.
Using 씨 with everyone. It can be neutral, distant, or awkward depending on workplace hierarchy.
Forgetting 님 in respectful titles such as 선배님, 사장님, 교수님.

usage: 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다.
께 and 여쭤보다 both add respect.
examples: 어르신도 계시면 도와드릴까요? 하고 물어볼게요.
If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'
Respectful presence plus polite help offer.
nuance: 어르신 is respectful and warm. 어른 simply means adult or grown-up; 어르신 adds social respect for age.
mistakes: Using 어른 when you need respectful tone. 어르신 is safer for elders.
Pairing 어르신 with 있다 in polite speech. Use 계시다: 어르신이 계세요.
Using 반말 around elders just because the setting is casual.

usage: to bring detergent as a housewarming gift
examples: 집들이 선물로 세제를 가져가도 괜찮아요.
It is okay to bring detergent as a housewarming gift.
Practical gift sentence.
nuance: 세제 is practical rather than fancy. In 집들이 culture, practical household gifts can feel considerate because they help the new home run smoothly.
mistakes: Confusing 세제 with 세금. 세제 is detergent; 세금 is tax.
Using it for soap in general. Soap is 비누; detergent is 세제.
Forgetting that gift role uses 로: 선물로 세제를 가져가요.

usage: thanks to you / thanks to the senior colleague
It went well thanks to you.
examples: 선배님 덕분에 분위기가 편해졌어요.
Thanks to you, the atmosphere became comfortable.
Positive cause in a social setting.
nuance: 덕분에 is for welcome causes. 때문에 often sounds neutral or negative, so 선배님 때문에 잘 됐어요 can sound like blame even with a good result.
mistakes: Using 때문에 to thank someone. Use 덕분에 for a positive cause.
Forgetting the person before 덕분에: 선배님 덕분에, 친구 덕분에.
Using 덕분에 for a bad result. For bad results, 때문에 is usually natural.

usage: to put a baby to sleep
The baby sleeps; someone else causes it.
to put someone to bed early
examples: 엄마가 아기를 재웠어요.
The mother put the baby to sleep.
Causative: the baby sleeps, the mother causes it.
nuance: 자다 is intransitive: 아기가 자요. 재우다 adds a causer: 엄마가 아기를 재워요.
mistakes: Saying 엄마가 아기를 자요. Use 재우다 when the mother puts the baby to sleep.
Forgetting the object/causee: 아기를 재우다.
Treating 재우다 as simply 'sleep.' The subject is not the sleeper.

english: to make someone laugh; to be funny
examples: 그 농담이 모두를 웃겼어요.
That joke made everyone laugh.
The joke is the causer.
nuance: 웃다 is what the person does; 웃기다 is what causes the laughing. In speech, 웃기다 also works like 'to be funny.'
mistakes: Using 웃다 when the subject is the joke. Say 농담이 웃겼어요, not 농담이 웃었어요.
Forgetting that 웃기다 can be casual and colloquial as 'funny.'
Mixing up 웃기다 with 울리다: one causes laughter, the other tears or ringing.

english: to make someone cry; to ring
examples: 그 영화가 저를 울렸어요.
That movie made me cry.
The film causes the crying.
nuance: 울다 is cry or ring by itself; 울리다 makes someone cry or makes a sound ring.
mistakes: Saying 영화가 울었어요 when the movie made you cry. Say 영화가 저를 울렸어요.
Forgetting the object in emotional causative: 저를/사람들을 울리다.
Confusing 울리다's two uses: emotional 'make cry' and sound 'ring.'

examples: 회의 중이라서 목소리를 낮췄어요.
I lowered my voice because we were in a meeting.
The subject causes the voice level to become lower.
nuance: 낮다 is an adjective, while 낮추다 is an action verb. Compare 소리가 낮아요 with 소리를 낮춰 주세요.
mistakes: Using 낮다 as an action: 소리를 낮아요 is wrong. Say 소리를 낮춰요.
Confusing 낮추다 with 내려가다. 내려가다 means go down; 낮추다 means lower something.
Forgetting the object marker: 목소리를 낮추다.

english: to reduce; to cut down on
usage: -는 것 turns the action into the object being reduced.
examples: 자기 전에 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이기로 했어요.
I decided to cut down on looking at my phone before sleeping.
-는 것 is the habit being reduced; -기로 했어요 reports the decision.
nuance: 줄이다 is transitive: you reduce something. 줄다 is intransitive: something decreases by itself.
mistakes: Using 줄다 for your own action: 지출을 줄어요 is wrong. Say 지출을 줄여요.
Forgetting the object: 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이다, not just 휴대폰 보다 줄이다.
Confusing 줄이다 with 낮추다. 낮추다 is lowering a level such as price, voice, or volume; 줄이다 is reducing amount or frequency.

english: to be natural; obvious; no wonder
examples: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
-네요 shows the speaker is realizing why the result makes sense.
nuance: 당연하다 can sound dismissive if used carelessly. 당연하네요 is softer than 당연해요 because it frames the comment as realization.
mistakes: Using 당연하다 to praise directly. For praise, say 잘하시네요; 당연하네요 explains why the result makes sense.
Forgetting that 당연히 is the adverb, while 당연하다 is the adjective.
Overusing 당연하지요 in formal situations; 당연하군요 or 그렇군요 can sound more measured.

examples: 이 보고서는 근거가 부족합니다.
This report lacks evidence.
Formal written 평가.
주장을 뒷받침할 근거를 제시해야 한다.
Evidence that supports the claim must be presented.
근거를 제시하다 is the basic formal writing frame.
자료의 출처가 분명해야 근거로 사용할 수 있다.
The source of the material must be clear for it to be used as evidence.
근거로 사용하다 marks the role of the material with 로.
nuance: 근거 is broader than 증거; 증거 often means proof/evidence, while 근거 can mean the basis for reasoning.
mistakes: Using 이유 when the writing needs evidence. 이유 is a reason; 근거 is supporting basis.
Saying 근거를 부족하다. The noun is subject: 근거가 부족하다.

examples: 따라서 결론을 다시 검토해야 합니다.
Therefore, the conclusion must be reviewed again.
따라서 links evidence to action.
자료를 분석한 뒤 결론을 내렸다.
After analyzing the material, a conclusion was drawn.
결론을 내리다 is the standard verb phrase.
근거가 약하면 결론도 설득력을 잃는다.
If the evidence is weak, the conclusion also loses persuasiveness.
Shows why 결론 depends on 근거 in argument writing.
nuance: 결론 is the end point of reasoning, not simply the ending of a story.
mistakes: Using 결말 for essays. 결말 is a story ending; 결론 is an argument conclusion.
Forgetting object marking in 결론을 내리다.

examples: 그러나 핵심 주장은 유지할 수 있습니다.
However, the main claim can be maintained.
그러나 marks contrast while 핵심 narrows the scope.
이 글의 핵심은 비용 문제가 아니라 안전 문제이다.
The key point of this piece is not cost but safety.
핵심은 A가 아니라 B이다 is a useful written contrast frame.
핵심 내용을 먼저 정리한 뒤 사례를 붙인다.
First organize the key content, then attach examples.
핵심 내용 naturally pairs with summary and outline work.
nuance: 핵심 is more formal and analytical than 중요한 부분.
mistakes: Using 핵심 for any detail. It should be central, not incidental.
Mixing 핵심 내용 and 핵심 주장 without deciding whether you mean content or claim.

examples: 결국 보고서의 핵심은 근거와 논리입니다.
Ultimately, the core of the report is evidence and reasoning.
결국 sums up the argument.
주장은 분명하지만 논리에 비약이 있다.
The claim is clear, but there is a leap in the reasoning.
논리에 비약이 있다 is the natural critique, not 논리가 비약하다.
두 문장 사이의 논리를 더 분명히 해야 한다.
The reasoning between the two sentences needs to be made clearer.
Useful when revising paragraph flow.
nuance: 논리 is the structure of reasoning, not simply an opinion.
mistakes: Using 논리 as a vague synonym for 생각. 생각 is thought; 논리 is reasoning.
Forgetting that 논리가 비약하다 is unnatural; say 논리에 비약이 있다.

examples: 반면에 사례 분석은 보완이 필요합니다.
In contrast, the case analysis needs supplementation.
반면에 contrasts one part of a report with another.
주장을 뒷받침하려면 구체적인 사례를 제시해야 한다.
To support a claim, concrete cases must be presented.
사례를 제시하다 is the report-writing counterpart to giving examples.
해외 사례와 국내 사례를 비교했다.
Foreign cases and domestic cases were compared.
사례 works well with comparative analysis.
nuance: 사례 is more formal than 예 and often implies a real case or representative example.
mistakes: Using 예 only in formal reports when 사례 would sound more analytical.
Forgetting object marking in 사례를 제시하다.

examples: 실험 결과가 가설을 뒷받침했다.
The experimental result supported the hypothesis.
Plain written -다 style.
연구자는 먼저 가설을 세운 뒤 자료를 수집했다.
The researcher first formed a hypothesis and then collected data.
가설을 세우다 is more natural than 가설을 만들다 in research writing.
새로운 자료는 기존 가설과 맞지 않았다.
The new data did not fit the existing hypothesis.
Shows 가설 as something evidence can support or challenge.
nuance: 가설 is not a casual guess; it is a testable proposition.
mistakes: Using 추측 when formal research writing needs 가설.
Saying 가설을 만들다 in academic prose; 가설을 세우다 is more standard.

examples: 따라서 이 이론은 유효하다고 볼 수 있다.
Therefore, this theory can be considered valid.
Formal conclusion after evidence.
이 이론은 여러 사례를 설명하는 데 도움이 된다.
This theory helps explain several cases.
이론 explains patterns across cases, not just one opinion.
현장 자료를 통해 이론을 검토했다.
The theory was reviewed through field data.
이론을 검토하다 links naturally to evidence-based writing.
nuance: 이론 is more structured than 생각 or 의견.
mistakes: Using 이론 for any personal idea. For a personal view, use 의견 or 생각.
Forgetting object marking in 이론을 적용하다.

examples: 그러나 예상되는 반론도 검토해야 한다.
However, expected counterarguments must also be reviewed.
그러나 introduces contrast in written prose.
반론을 예상하지 않으면 글의 설득력이 약해진다.
If counterarguments are not anticipated, the writing becomes less persuasive.
Good argument writing handles objections before the reader raises them.
학생들은 서로의 주장에 대해 반론을 제기했다.
The students raised counterarguments against each other's claims.
반론을 제기하다 is the standard formal verb phrase.
nuance: 반론 is an argument against a claim; 반대 is broader opposition.
mistakes: Using 반대 when the text specifically needs a counterargument.
Forgetting the object marker in 반론을 제기하다.

examples: 이 댓글 완전 웃겨 ㅋㅋ.
This comment is so funny lol.
완전 fits casual peer chat.
그 영상 완전 레전드야.
That video is totally legendary.
완전 naturally intensifies slang like 레전드.
공식 글에서는 완전보다 매우나 상당히가 자연스럽다.
In official writing, 매우 or 상당히 is more natural than 완전.
The key lesson is register control.
nuance: 완전 literally means complete, but in casual speech it works as a general booster. It can sound youthful, excited, or blunt depending on context.
mistakes: Using 완전 in essays or official notices where 매우, 상당히, or 매우 are safer.
Assuming 완전 always means completely in a literal sense; in chat it often just means really.
Stacking too many boosters such as 완전 진짜 너무 in one sentence unless the tone is intentionally playful.

usage: Casual reaction after a live stream or show.
examples: 그 댓글 반응 레전드다.
The reaction to that comment is legendary.
Plain exclamatory -다 works in casual online reactions.
오늘 라이브 채팅 레전드였어.
Today's live chat was legendary.
Natural after an especially chaotic or funny stream.
공식 보고서에는 레전드라는 표현을 쓰지 않는다.
The expression 레전드 is not used in official reports.
Slang recognition includes knowing where not to use it.
nuance: 레전드 can praise something impressive, but it can also be ironic when something is absurd or unbelievably bad.
mistakes: Treating 레전드 as only positive. Online use can be ironic.
Using 레전드 in formal writing where 유명한 사례, 대표적 사례, or 대단한 would fit better.
Adding honorifics directly to slang to make it formal. 레전드세요 is not a safe formal upgrade.

examples: 이 댓글 개웃겨 ㅋㅋㅋ.
This comment is hilarious lolol.
Natural only in very casual text.
친구한테는 개웃겨라고 해도 되지만 교수님께는 정말 재미있었습니다라고 해야 한다.
You can say 개웃겨 to a friend, but to a professor you should say 정말 재미있었습니다.
The same reaction needs a different register.
단톡방에서는 개웃겨가 자연스럽지만 회사 공지에는 맞지 않는다.
개웃겨 is natural in a group chat, but it does not fit a company notice.
Register boundary.
nuance: 개웃겨 is stronger and rougher than 너무 웃겨 or 진짜 웃겨. It can sound friendly, but it can also sound careless if the relationship is not close.
mistakes: Using 개웃겨 because it means funny without noticing the rough casual prefix 개-.
Trying to make it polite with 요. 개웃겨요 is possible among close peers but still slangy, not formal.
Using it about sensitive topics; the strong casual tone can sound dismissive.

usage: the live chat is too fast
examples: 라이브 채팅이 너무 빨라서 댓글을 다 못 읽었어.
The live chat was so fast that I couldn't read all the comments.
Digital scenario for this chapter.
라이브 채팅에는 ㅋㅋ와 ㅇㅈ 같은 반응이 자주 올라온다.
Reactions like ㅋㅋ and ㅇㅈ often appear in live chat.
Connects the digital place to the slang forms.
공식 문의는 라이브 채팅보다 이메일로 남기는 것이 안전하다.
For official inquiries, leaving an email is safer than using live chat.
Register and channel choice matter.
nuance: 라이브 채팅 is a channel, not a writing style. It invites short reactions, abbreviations, and fast turn-taking.
mistakes: Assuming live-chat slang transfers to email or official posts.
Using 댓글 for every chat line; 댓글 is a comment, while 라이브 채팅 is the live chat space.
Overusing abbreviations when the chat is customer support or official service chat.

usage: Use 이/가 because 입자 is the subject.
examples: 이 문장은 입자를 다시 확인해야 해요.
This sentence needs its particles checked again.
Useful when reviewing learner output.
면접 답변에서는 입자 하나도 어색하게 들릴 수 있어요.
In an interview answer, even one particle can sound awkward.
Shows why production review matters.
이유는 맞지만 입자가 틀려서 문장이 부자연스러워요.
The reason is right, but the sentence sounds unnatural because the particle is wrong.
Meaning and grammar both matter.
nuance: 입자 is the technical grammar term. In class it helps learners talk about the exact small piece that changed the sentence.
mistakes: Ignoring particles because the main vocabulary is correct.
Using 은/는 and 이/가 as simple English subject markers instead of discourse choices.
Changing a noun without rechecking whether the particle still fits.

examples: 이미 끝난 일이라면 시제를 과거로 바꿔야 해요.
If it is something already finished, you need to change the tense to past.
Connects time meaning to ending choice.
이메일을 보내기 전에 시제와 높임말을 같이 확인했어요.
Before sending the email, I checked the tense and honorific language together.
Tense and register are reviewed together.
경험을 말할 때 시제가 흔들리면 답변이 불안정하게 들려요.
When talking about experience, if the tense wavers, the answer sounds unstable.
Interview and storytelling context.
